patient_information: A 53-year-old Malawian man, who works as a subsistence farmer, presents with a new diagnosis of HIV infection and advanced immunosuppression (CD4 count not specified). His past medical history is unremarkable, he is not on any regular medication, and is a non-smoker.
chief_complaint: Productive cough with whitish sputum for 3 months.
history_of_present_illness: The patient has had a productive cough with whitish sputum for 3 months, accompanied by night sweats and unquantified weight loss. Two months prior to presentation, he was seen at a health centre for the same complaints and was given presumptive antimalarials and a 5-day course of amoxicillin, with no improvement. He is not aware of any tuberculosis (TB) contacts.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is a subsistence farmer in Malawi. He has never worked in a mine or the construction industry. He is married with five children, all of whom are well.
vitals: On admission, his temperature was 38.8°C (101.8°F), blood pressure was 100/80 mmHg, pulse was 88 bpm, and oxygen saturation was 97% on ambient air.
physical_exam: The patient appeared slightly wasted and mildly anaemic. Examination of his mouth revealed no oral thrush, Kaposi’s sarcoma, or oral hairy leukoplakia. His chest was clear on auscultation, and heart sounds were normal without murmurs. There was no lymphadenopathy, and his liver and spleen were not enlarged.
labs_and_diagnostics: An HIV test was reactive. His white blood cell count was low at 3.2 x 10^9/L, and haemoglobin was 9.8 g/dL. Two sputum samples were negative for acid-fast bacilli (AFB), and induced sputum was also negative for AFB. A malaria RDT and a thick smear for Plasmodium spp. were both negative. Sputum PCR was not available. A chest radiograph on admission showed a prominent hilar region bilaterally but was otherwise normal. An exercise test was negative, with oxygen saturation rising from 97% to 98%.
differential_diagnosis: The primary suspected diagnosis was smear-negative pulmonary tuberculosis (TB), given the patient's HIV-positive status, advanced immunosuppression, and chronic constitutional symptoms unresponsive to antibiotics. Other considerations included Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) due to the immunosuppression. A concomitant bacterial chest infection was considered less likely to explain the 3-month illness duration. Pulmonary Kaposi's sarcoma was deemed unlikely due to the absence of skin or oral lesions and typical radiographic findings. Gram-negative sepsis secondary to invasive non-typhoidal Salmonellae was also considered in this febrile, anaemic, and immunosuppressed patient.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient was initially treated with intravenous ceftriaxone and oral erythromycin for a possible bacterial infection, but his fever persisted despite a slight subjective improvement in his cough. He also received a prophylactic dose of co-trimoxazole. On day 7 of admission, he was started on empirical treatment for smear-negative TB with a four-drug regimen of Isoniazid, Rifampicin, Pyrazinamide, and Ethambutol. After the first week of antituberculous treatment, he began to feel better, his fever resolved, and the cough gradually settled. He was discharged home and started antiretroviral therapy three weeks into his TB treatment.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis is smear-negative pulmonary tuberculosis. This conclusion is based on the patient's clinical presentation of chronic cough, weight loss, and night sweats in the context of newly diagnosed HIV with advanced immunosuppression. The diagnosis was supported by the failure of broad-spectrum antibiotics and the definitive clinical response, including resolution of fever and cough, after starting empirical four-drug antituberculous therapy. Although sputum smears for acid-fast bacilli were negative and advanced diagnostics were unavailable, the clinical and epidemiological context strongly pointed to TB, which is a common presentation in this patient population.
